newsitem.title: USA: Growth in U.S. May consumer credit slows.
newsitem.headline: Growth in U.S. May consumer credit slows.

text.p: U.S. consumer installment credit rose in May by $3 billion, or at a 2.9 percent annual rate, following a revised $9.7-billion increase in April at a 9.7 percent rate, the Federal Reserve said on Tuesday.
May's increase was smaller than the $5.6-billion rise forecast by Wall Street analysts.

The April increase in consumer credit remained the largest monthly pickup since a revised $9.9-billion jump in January and was much stronger than Wall Street economists' forecasts for a $4.3-billion rise.
Previously, the Fed said April consumer credit grew by $7.6 billion but it revised that estimate up. The Fed revised the monthly consumer credit figures back to December.
As a result, it said February consumer credit grew by $6.3 billion instead of by $6.7 billion and that March consumer credit increased $2.7 billion rather than $3.1 billion.

In May, auto credit outstanding shrank by $1.7 billion at a 5.4 percent annual rate -- the biggest drop since a $7.2-billion plunge in October 1992. That followed a $4.5-billion surge at a 14.5 percent rate in April auto credit.
Revolving, or credit-card, credit rose by $700 million at a 1.8 percent annual rate in May, the Fed said. Credit-card debt had risen $5.4 billion at a 13.4 percent rate in April.

Other credit, which includes consumer bank loans like those for mobile homes and to pay for education but not real estate mortgages, jumped $4 billion at a 13.3 percent annual rate in May. In April, this category of credit fell $100 million at an 0.3 percent annual rate.
Before seasonal adjustment, total outstanding consumer credit in May was $1.214 trillion, up from $1.139 trillion a year earlier in May 1996.
